q: Inside a JuMP solver-independent lazy-constraint callback with argument cb_data, the current solution violates $x\le 2$. Which code correctly adds this constraint?
options: @constraint(model, x <= 2)
con = @build_constraint(x <= 2) followed by MOI.submit(model, MOI.UserCut(cb_data), con)
con = @build_constraint(x <= 2) followed by MOI.submit(model, MOI.LazyConstraint(cb_data), con)
set_upper_bound(x, 2)
explain: The constraint object is built with @build_constraint and submitted as MOI.LazyConstraint(cb_data); the callback itself is registered with set_attribute(model, MOI.LazyConstraintCallback(), f). Calling @constraint or changing bounds inside a callback is undefined behaviour, and a user cut is not allowed to remove integer-feasible points.

source.label: JuMP manual — Solver-independent Callbacks

q: Inside a JuMP solver-independent callback it is safe to call @constraint(model, ...) or to change a variable bound, provided the model stays feasible.
explain: Inside a callback only callback_node_status, callback_value, @build_constraint and MOI.submit may be used. Any other use of the JuMP API there is undefined behaviour and may cause errors, wrong answers or a crash. Also, each callback type can be set only once (a second set_attribute overwrites the first).

source.label: JuMP manual — Solver-independent Callbacks

q: In a branch-and-cut code for the TSP (JuMP with Gurobi) the model initially contains only the degree constraints. Explain why the subtour-elimination separator must be registered as a lazy constraint callback and not (only) as a user cut callback.
model: User cuts are only allowed to remove fractional LP points: they must not cut off any integer-feasible point of the model as stated, and the solver is free to ignore them or not to call the callback at every solution. Subtour constraints do change the set of integer-feasible points: an integer solution made of several subtours satisfies the degree constraints and would be accepted as feasible. They are part of the problem definition, so they must be submitted as lazy constraints, which are checked for candidate integer solutions. (Subtour inequalities may additionally be separated at fractional points to strengthen the bound.)
rubric: User cuts may only cut off fractional points, never integer-feasible points of the current model
Integer solutions consisting of several subtours are feasible for the initial model
Subtour constraints define feasibility, hence lazy constraints
The solver may ignore user cuts, so correctness cannot depend on them

source.label: JuMP manual — Solver-independent Callbacks

q: In JuMP and Gurobi, a user cut is allowed to remove an integer-feasible solution of the model, as long as that solution is not optimal.
explain: User cuts must not remove any integer-feasible point, optimal or not; they may only cut off fractional LP solutions. A constraint that removes integer points must be submitted as a lazy constraint; otherwise the solver can return wrong answers.

source.label: JuMP manual — Solver-independent Callbacks

q: In a JuMP lazy-constraint callback, a point shows up that violates a lazy constraint you already submitted earlier in the same solve. According to the JuMP manual, what is the right reaction?
options: Submit the violated constraint again: the solver may revisit such a point (for example because the constraint was removed during presolve)
Ignore it: a lazy constraint submitted once is guaranteed to stay in the model
Stop the solve, because this indicates a bug in the solver
Submit it as a user cut instead, since a lazy constraint can only be added once
explain: There is no guarantee that an earlier lazy constraint is still active, so the callback must cut off a violating point every time it sees one. Conversely, a lazy constraint should only be submitted when the current callback solution actually violates it; the callback may be invoked at fractional or integer nodes (query callback_node_status).

source.label: JuMP manual — Solver-independent Callbacks

q: JuMP: after optimize!(model), which functions tell you (a) why the solver stopped, (b) whether a solution is available, (c) the incumbent value, the best bound and the gap?
a:
(a) termination_status(model): OPTIMAL, INFEASIBLE, DUAL_INFEASIBLE (unbounded if a primal feasible point exists), INFEASIBLE_OR_UNBOUNDED, or a limit such as TIME_LIMIT, NODE_LIMIT, SOLUTION_LIMIT; raw_status(model) gives the solver's own message.
(b) primal_status(model) (e.g. FEASIBLE_POINT), dual_status(model), result_count(model); shortcut is_solved_and_feasible(model).
(c) objective_value(model) = value of the best primal solution (incumbent); objective_bound(model) = best known bound on the optimum (the dual bound of branch and bound); relative_gap(model). Work counters: solve_time, node_count, simplex_iterations.
Values: value(x), dual(c), shadow_price(c), reduced_cost(x). Query everything before modifying the model: a modification resets it to OPTIMIZE_NOT_CALLED.

source.label: JuMP manual — Solutions (querying status, bounds, gap)

q: A JuMP/Gurobi run of a minimisation MIP stops with termination_status == TIME_LIMIT, primal_status == FEASIBLE_POINT, objective_value = 120 and objective_bound = 100. What can you conclude?
options: The optimal value is 100; the solution of cost 120 only needs to be rounded
Nothing: after a time limit neither number is meaningful
A feasible solution of cost 100 is known and no solution can cost more than 120
A feasible solution of cost 120 is known and the optimal value lies in $[100,120]$: the incumbent is at most 20 above optimal
explain: objective_value is the incumbent (primal bound, an upper bound for a min problem) and objective_bound the best dual (lower) bound from branch and bound. So $100\le z^*\le 120$; the absolute gap is 20 and the relative gap is $|120-100|/|120|\approx 0.167$ (16.7 percent) with the usual solver definition.

source.label: JuMP manual — Solutions (querying status, bounds, gap)

q: In JuMP, if termination_status(model) is TIME_LIMIT, a feasible solution is always available, so value(x) can be called without further checks.
explain: A limit status only says why the solver stopped; it does not say whether an incumbent exists. Check primal_status(model) == FEASIBLE_POINT before calling value.

source.label: JuMP manual — Solutions (querying status, bounds, gap)

q: The JuMP TSP tutorial solves the same instance twice: (1) iteratively: optimize!, find a subtour, add it with @constraint, re-optimize, repeat; (2) with a lazy-constraint callback. Both reach the same optimal tour, but in the tutorial's run (2) was about 1.85 times faster. Why?
options: The callback version uses a stronger formulation with MTZ constraints
In (1) the MIP is solved again from scratch after every added constraint, while in (2) a single branch-and-bound search keeps its tree, cuts and incumbent
The callback version adds all subtour elimination constraints before the solve starts
The iterative version only solves LP relaxations and therefore needs more iterations
explain: Row generation by re-solving restarts branch and bound each time. The lazy callback checks integer nodes (callback_node_status(cb_data, model) == MOI.CALLBACK_NODE_STATUS_INTEGER), reads the point with callback_value, extracts the shortest cycle and, if it is shorter than $n$, submits $\sum_{i \lt j,\ i,j\in S}x_{ij}\le |S|-1$ inside the one running search.

source.label: JuMP tutorial — Traveling Salesperson Problem (lazy constraints)

q: You have computed a nearest-neighbour tour and want Gurobi, called through JuMP, to start from it. How do you pass it to the solver?
options: Add @constraint(model, x[i,j] == 1) for every edge of the tour
Call fix(x[i,j], 1.0) for every edge of the tour
Call set_start_value(x[i,j], 1.0) (or 0.0) on the model variables before optimize!; Gurobi receives it as a MIP start
Set the parameter Cutoff to the tour length; this loads the tour as incumbent
explain: Start values, given with @variable(model, y, start = 1) or set_start_value, are passed to a MIP solver as a MIP start: a candidate incumbent that the solver checks and, if necessary, completes. Fixing variables or adding equalities would force the tour instead of suggesting it; a cutoff only declares worse solutions uninteresting, it does not supply a solution.

source.label: JuMP manual — Variables (start values, fixing, integrality)

q: JuMP with Gurobi: how do you create the model, set a time limit of 100 seconds and a 1 percent relative MIP gap, and what extra steps does a Gurobi-specific lazy-constraint callback need?
a:
model = Model(Gurobi.Optimizer)
set_attribute(model, "TimeLimit", 100)
set_attribute(model, "MIPGap", 0.01) (similarly set_attribute(model, "Presolve", 0))
Solver-specific callback: MOI.set(model, MOI.RawOptimizerAttribute("LazyConstraints"), 1), then MOI.set(model, Gurobi.CallbackFunction(), f) with f(cb_data, cb_where::Cint); inside, test cb_where == GRB_CB_MIPSOL and call Gurobi.load_callback_variable_primal(cb_data, cb_where) before callback_value(cb_data, x), then MOI.submit(model, MOI.LazyConstraint(cb_data), con). With the solver-independent MOI.LazyConstraintCallback this bookkeeping is done for you.

source.label: Gurobi.jl package page in the JuMP documentation

q: A Gurobi log for a minimisation MIP shows at the root node Incumbent = 157344.610 and BestBd = 38893.9036. What value, in percent, is printed in the Gap column?
explain: Gap $=|\text{Incumbent}-\text{BestBd}|/|\text{Incumbent}|=(157344.610-38893.9036)/157344.610=0.7528$, printed as 75.3%. The incumbent is the primal (upper) bound; BestBd is the dual (lower) bound, here the root LP value.

source.label: Gurobi Optimizer reference — MIP Logging (v13.0)

q:
Two consecutive lines of a Gurobi log for a minimisation MIP (columns: Expl Unexpl | Obj Depth IntInf | Incumbent BestBd Gap | It/Node Time):
     0     0 38893.9036    0   11 157344.610 38893.9036  75.3%     -    0s
H    0     0                    80297.610430 38893.9036  51.6%     -    0s
What happened between the two lines?
options: Branching produced an integral node and the bound improved to 80297.61
A MIP heuristic found a new incumbent of value 80297.61; the bound is unchanged, so the gap drops to $(80297.61-38893.90)/80297.61\approx 0.516$
A cutting plane raised the lower bound from 38893.90 to 80297.61
The solver halted (H) after exploring 51.6% of the nodes
explain: A leading H marks a new incumbent found by a heuristic; a leading * marks one found by branching (an integral node relaxation). Only the Incumbent column changes; BestBd stays at the root LP value 38893.90, where 11 integer variables were still fractional (IntInf = 11).

source.label: Gurobi Optimizer reference — MIP Logging (v13.0)

q: Gurobi MIP log: what do the columns Expl, Unexpl, Obj, Depth, IntInf, Incumbent, BestBd, Gap, It/Node mean, and what are the three parts of the log?
a:
• Expl: nodes explored so far; Unexpl: leaf nodes still open.
  • Obj: relaxation objective of the current node; Depth: its depth in the tree; IntInf: number of integer variables with fractional values in that relaxation.
  • Incumbent: objective of the best feasible solution (primal bound); BestBd: bound given by the open nodes (dual bound); Gap: relative gap between the two.
  • It/Node: average simplex iterations per node; Time: elapsed seconds.
A leading H = incumbent found by a heuristic, * = incumbent found by branching. The log has a presolve section, a progress (branch-and-cut) section and a summary section; the 'Cutting planes' block lists by type (Gomory, MIR, cover, ...) the cuts still present in the LP relaxation at the end of the search.

source.label: Gurobi Optimizer reference — MIP Logging (v13.0)

q:
A Gurobi log ends with:
Optimal solution found (tolerance 1.00e-04)
Best objective 4.000505414200e+04, best bound 4.000505414200e+04, gap 0.0000%
What does 'tolerance 1.00e-04' refer to?
options: The relative MIP gap (parameter MIPGap): the search stops, and the incumbent is reported as optimal, once the gap between best objective and best bound falls below $10^{-4}$
The integrality tolerance: values within $10^{-4}$ of an integer count as integral
The feasibility tolerance of the simplex method
The fraction of the runtime spent in heuristics
explain: Gurobi stops when the relative gap between incumbent and best bound is below MIPGap. 'Optimal' therefore means optimal within this tolerance; in this log the two values happen to coincide (gap 0.0000%). MIPGapAbs plays the same role for the absolute gap.

source.label: Gurobi Optimizer reference — MIP Logging (v13.0)

q: Gurobi: which parameters control when a MIP solve stops, and what do Cutoff, MIPFocus, ImproveStartTime and Cuts do?
a:
Stopping: TimeLimit (wall clock; can make runs non-deterministic) or WorkLimit (deterministic); MIPGap (relative) and MIPGapAbs (absolute) gap between best solution and best bound; NodeLimit, IterationLimit, SolutionLimit; BestObjStop / BestBdStop (stop on the primal or the dual bound alone).
Cutoff: solutions with objective worse than the given value are of no interest.
MIPFocus: 1 = find good feasible solutions quickly; 2 = concentrate on proving optimality; 3 = concentrate on the bound.
ImproveStartGap / ImproveStartTime: at a chosen gap or time, give up on moving the bound and devote all effort to finding better feasible solutions.
Cuts: aggressiveness of cutting planes (very easy models may gain from turning cuts off, very hard ones from aggressive cuts).

source.label: Gurobi Optimizer reference — Parameter guidelines

q: Gurobi finds a good incumbent early, but the best bound hardly moves and the gap stays large. Which MIPFocus setting does Gurobi's parameter guideline recommend trying in this situation?
options: MIPFocus = 1
MIPFocus = 3
MIPFocus = 0 together with a larger Heuristics value
MIPFocus = 1 together with ImproveStartTime = 0
explain: MIPFocus = 3 concentrates on the bound and is the setting recommended when the best bound moves very slowly or not at all. MIPFocus = 1 favours finding feasible solutions quickly (2 favours proving optimality). More heuristic effort or the improvement mode only help the primal side, which is not the problem here.

source.label: Gurobi Optimizer reference — Parameter guidelines

q: What does Gurobi's Heuristics parameter control, and what is its default?
options: The desired fraction of total MIP runtime spent in primal heuristics; default 0.05 (5 percent)
The number of heuristic solutions kept in the solution pool; default 10
Which single heuristic (RINS, feasibility pump, ...) is used; default automatic
The relative gap at which heuristics are switched off; default $10^{-4}$
explain: Raising Heuristics can produce more and better feasible solutions, at the expense of progress on the bound. Related parameters: NoRelHeurTime (a heuristic that searches for good solutions without solving the LP relaxation), and MinRelNodes, PumpPasses (feasibility pump), ZeroObjNodes: expensive heuristics to try when no feasible solution is being found.

source.label: Gurobi Optimizer reference — Parameters (reference page)

q: Gurobi callbacks are invoked with a where code: MIPSOL (a new integer solution was found) or MIPNODE (a node of the tree is being explored), among others. From which of them may user cuts (addCut) and lazy constraints (addLazy) be added?
options: addCut: MIPSOL only; addLazy: MIPNODE only
Both from any callback, including PRESOLVE and SIMPLEX
Both only from MIPSOL
addCut: MIPNODE only; addLazy: MIPNODE or MIPSOL
explain: User cuts tighten the LP relaxation of a node, so they are added at MIPNODE; they must be true cutting planes that never cut off an integer solution feasible for the original model (Gurobi advises PreCrush = 1 when adding your own cuts). Lazy constraints can be added at MIPNODE or MIPSOL and require the parameter LazyConstraints to be set. The point is read with getSolution() in MIPSOL and with getNodeRel() in MIPNODE (only when the node status is optimal).

source.label: Gurobi Optimizer reference — C++ API, GRBCallback

q: You implement subtour elimination for the TSP in a Gurobi callback. (a) Which where code must be handled, and which parameter must be set? (b) May you additionally separate subtour inequalities at fractional node solutions, and how? (c) Could you drop the integer-solution check and rely on fractional separation with user cuts only?
model:
(a) Handle MIPSOL: every new integer solution must be checked for subtours (read it with getSolution) and a violated subtour constraint added with addLazy; the parameter LazyConstraints = 1 must be set.
(b) Yes, optionally at MIPNODE when the node relaxation has been solved to optimality (read it with getNodeRel): submit the violated inequalities as lazy constraints or, since subtour inequalities are valid for all tours, as user cuts with addCut (then PreCrush = 1 is advised).
(c) No. User cuts are not allowed to define the feasible set, so integer solutions containing subtours would still be accepted; the MIPSOL check with lazy constraints cannot be dropped.
rubric: MIPSOL callback checks every new integer solution
Fractional separation at MIPNODE is optional (lazy constraints, or user cuts via addCut with PreCrush)
User cuts alone cannot define feasibility, so the MIPSOL check is mandatory

source.label: Gurobi Optimizer reference — C++ API, GRBCallback

q: You give Gurobi a MIP start and the log prints User MIP start produced solution with objective 1250. What does this message mean?
options: The start was infeasible and was discarded
The start was feasible exactly as given
Gurobi had to repair or complete the start (for example only some variables had values) and obtained a feasible solution of objective 1250
Gurobi proved that 1250 is the optimal value
explain: Loaded user MIP start with objective ... is printed when the start is feasible as given; User MIP start produced solution with objective ... when Gurobi had to repair or complete it; User MIP start did not produce a new incumbent solution when that fails. A MIP start only supplies an incumbent; it proves nothing about optimality.

source.label: Gurobi Optimizer reference — Warm Start Options (v13.0)

q: A MIP start passed to Gurobi specifies values for only some of the integer variables. What does Gurobi do with it?
options: It rejects the start: every variable must have a value
It sets every unspecified variable to 0
It fixes the specified variables for the whole search
It tries to complete the start by solving a sub-MIP over the unspecified variables, with effort limited by the parameter StartNodeLimit
explain: Partial starts are allowed; the completion is a possibly expensive sub-MIP whose node budget is StartNodeLimit (by default the same as SubMIPNodes). A start is a suggestion used to build one feasible solution, not a fixing. Variable hints (VarHintVal, VarHintPri) are different: they guide heuristics and branching during the whole search.

source.label: Gurobi Optimizer reference — Warm Start Options (v13.0)

q: Gurobi's guidance on MIP starts: it is enough to supply start values for (some of) the binary/integer variables; also supplying values for the continuous variables is generally discouraged.
explain: Gurobi completes the start by computing the remaining variables itself. Values for continuous variables are discouraged because small numerical inconsistencies can cause the start to be rejected. Also, a MIP start can reduce solve time but there is no guarantee that it does.

source.label: Gurobi Help Center — "How do I use MIP starts?"

q: Which of these large-neighbourhood-search heuristics is a start heuristic, i.e. can run before any feasible solution is known?
options: RINS
RENS
Local branching
Crossover
explain: RENS uses only the LP optimum $\bar x$: it fixes every integer variable that is already integral in $\bar x$, restricts each fractional one to $\{\lfloor\bar x_j\rfloor,\lceil\bar x_j\rceil\}$ and solves the resulting sub-MIP. RINS needs the incumbent as a second reference point, local branching searches around the incumbent, and crossover combines several feasible solutions: all three are improvement heuristics.

source.label: Primal Heuristics — "When MIP solvers roll dice" (T. Berthold, CO@Work 2024 slides)

q: What does the RINS heuristic (Danna et al. 2005) do?
options: It rounds every fractional variable of the LP optimum to the nearest integer
It fixes the variables whose values agree in the LP optimum $\bar x$ and in the incumbent $\tilde x$, and solves the remaining sub-MIP
It fixes the variables whose values agree in all of several known integer solutions, and solves the remaining sub-MIP
It adds the constraint $\sum_j|x_j-\tilde x_j|\le k$ around the incumbent $\tilde x$ and solves the resulting MIP
explain: RINS uses two reference points: being close to the LP optimum suggests good quality, being close to the incumbent suggests feasibility. Fixing what several integer solutions share is crossover, a distance constraint around the incumbent is local branching, and rounding without solving a sub-MIP is a plain rounding heuristic.

source.label: Primal Heuristics — "When MIP solvers roll dice" (T. Berthold, CO@Work 2024 slides)

q: Local branching (Fischetti and Lodi 2003) searches a neighbourhood of the incumbent $\tilde x$. How is this neighbourhood defined?
options: By the constraint $\Delta(x,\tilde x)=\sum_j|x_j-\tilde x_j|\le k$ (the 1-norm distance to the incumbent is at most $k$)
By fixing all variables that are integral in the LP optimum
By fixing the variables on which the LP optimum and the incumbent agree
By fixing the variables on which several incumbents agree
explain: Local branching adds a bound on the 1-norm distance to the incumbent and lets the MIP solver search that neighbourhood; it was originally proposed as a branching strategy. Fixing LP-integral variables is RENS, fixing what LP optimum and incumbent share is RINS, fixing what several solutions share is crossover.

source.label: Primal Heuristics — "When MIP solvers roll dice" (T. Berthold, CO@Work 2024 slides)

q: What is the idea of the Crossover heuristic in MIP solvers?
options: Fix the variables that coincide in the incumbent and in the LP optimum, then solve the sub-MIP
Add one constraint per fractional variable of the LP optimum
Fix the variables that take the same value in all of several feasible integer solutions, then solve the sub-MIP
explain: Crossover (Rothberg 2007) comes from a genetic algorithm: several feasible solutions are combined by fixing what they all agree on and optimising over the rest (paired with a mutation step). Fixing what the incumbent and the LP optimum share is RINS.

source.label: Primal Heuristics — "When MIP solvers roll dice" (T. Berthold, CO@Work 2024 slides)

q: Describe the feasibility pump heuristic step by step.
a:
1. Solve the LP relaxation.
  2. Round the LP optimum to an integer point $\tilde x$.
  3. If $\tilde x$ is feasible, stop.
  4. If the procedure is cycling, perturb.
  5. Replace the objective by the distance $\Delta(x,\tilde x)=\sum_j|x_j-\tilde x_j|$.
  6. Solve this LP (a projection of $\tilde x$ back onto the LP polyhedron).
  7. Go to step 2.
It alternates between a point that is integral but possibly infeasible and a point that is LP-feasible but possibly fractional. Variants: auxiliary distance variables for general integers; the objective feasibility pump mixes the original objective with the distance; FP 2.0 adds propagation after each rounding.

source.label: Primal Heuristics — "When MIP solvers roll dice" (T. Berthold, CO@Work 2024 slides)

q: Diving heuristics in a MIP solver ...
options: simulate a depth-first search in the branch-and-bound tree: fix variables, re-solve the LP, repeat
change the objective function
manipulate the simplex algorithm
explain: A dive repeatedly fixes (rounds) a variable and re-solves the LP, like one root-to-leaf path of the tree. Variants differ in the variable chosen: fractional diving (least fractional variable), guided diving (round towards the incumbent), coefficient diving (direction with fewer locks), vector-length diving. Changing the objective is the feasibility-pump idea. Rule of thumb from the slides: good branching rules make bad diving rules.

source.label: Primal Heuristics — "When MIP solvers roll dice" (T. Berthold, CO@Work 2024 slides)

q: Which statement about primal heuristics inside a MIP solver is correct?
options: They typically come with an approximation ratio
They might terminate unsuccessfully, without finding any solution
They always improve the primal bound when they are called
explain: Primal heuristics are incomplete methods: they often find good solutions quickly but give no guarantee of success or quality. Their role inside an exact solver: proving feasibility, providing near-optimal solutions that often suffice in practice, and supplying an incumbent that prunes the rest of the search.

source.label: Primal Heuristics — "When MIP solvers roll dice" (T. Berthold, CO@Work 2024 slides)

q: The primal-dual integral, used to measure how well a solver (and its heuristics) performs over time, ...
options: takes every update of the incumbent (and of the bound) over time into account, rewarding good solutions found early
depends on the number of processed branch-and-bound nodes
measures only the time needed to find a first feasible solution
explain: It accounts for each improvement of the incumbent and of the dual bound at the moment it happens, so finding good solutions early is rewarded. It is neither a node count nor just the time to the first solution.

source.label: Primal Heuristics — "When MIP solvers roll dice" (T. Berthold, CO@Work 2024 slides)

q: Classic local search versus large neighbourhood search (LNS): what is the difference? Name the main classes of primal heuristics in MIP solvers.
a:
Local search explores a small neighbourhood explicitly (a $k$-exchange neighbourhood costs about $O(n^k)$ to scan; Lin–Kernighan is the classic TSP example), accepts improving moves and stops in a local optimum unless some worsening moves are allowed.
LNS defines a neighbourhood too large to enumerate (fix variables or add a constraint) and searches it by partially solving a sub-MIP: RENS, RINS, local branching, crossover.
Classes in MIP solvers: rounding (make an LP solution integral without re-optimising), diving (fix variables, re-solve the LP), feasibility-pump / objective diving (change the objective to reduce fractionality), large neighbourhood search, pivoting.
Start heuristics need no incumbent and usually run early from the LP optimum; improvement heuristics need a feasible solution and try to improve it.

source.label: Primal Heuristics — "When MIP solvers roll dice" (T. Berthold, CO@Work 2024 slides)

q: JuMP: what is the difference between dual(c) and shadow_price(c), and what is reduced_cost(x) used for in the Benders tutorial?
a:
dual(c) uses JuMP's own sign convention, which depends on the direction of the constraint ($\le$, $\ge$, $=$) and not on whether the model is a minimisation or a maximisation. shadow_price(c) returns the dual with the textbook sensitivity sign.
reduced_cost(x) is the reduced cost of a variable; in the JuMP Benders tutorial the subproblem contains copy variables fixed to the first-stage values, and their reduced costs are used as the subgradient $\pi$ in the cut $\theta\ge V_2(x_k)+\pi^\top(x-x_k)$.
All of these need a dual solution: check dual_status(model), or use is_solved_and_feasible(model; dual = true).
